text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • First-line medical therapy: high-volume saline irrigation twice daily and fluticasone nasal spray two sprays in each nostril daily, with technique taught in clinic; topical decongestant sprays stopped because rebound blockage follows use beyond a few days
  • Otolaryngology consultation with nasal endoscopy to confirm the diagnosis with objective evidence and to look for nasal polyps, and advice on further treatment, imaging, and surgery
  • Check for conditions that change management (asthma, cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, ciliary dyskinesia, aspirin sensitivity, a dental source): history, blood eosinophils and total IgE; no imaging and no antifungal treatment at this stage
  • Fitness to fly: no flying while blocked or in pain, as 14 CFR 61.53 requires; a 48-hour ground trial before flying on any new medicine; only medicines the FAA accepts for pilots (nasal steroid sprays, saline, non-sedating antihistamines, pseudoephedrine); the diphenhydramine night tablet stopped, with at least 60 hours before flying after any dose; and practice of ear and sinus clearing on descent
  • Culture-directed antibiotic for the acute exacerbation with pus in the middle meatus: an endoscopically guided culture and amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days; no oral corticosteroid, because her disease has no polyps; no long-term antibiotic
  • CT of the sinuses after at least eight weeks of irrigation and nasal steroid plus the antibiotic course, with the SNOT-22 repeated, to decide whether endoscopic sinus surgery is appropriate and to plan it
  • Endoscopic sinus surgery on the left (maxillary antrostomy, anterior ethmoidectomy, and frontal recess dissection), chosen by her after a shared decision because the SNOT-22 stayed above 20 with disease on CT after appropriate medical therapy; then budesonide added to the saline rinse, cleaning of the sinuses in the ear, nose and throat clinic, and no flying until the surgeon clears her

resource.title: Amelia Earhart synthetic care plan
resource.description: Primary care for a 25-year-old private pilot with chronic sinus symptoms: diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis by symptoms plus objective evidence (nasal endoscopy), the SNOT-22 symptom score, a check for conditions that change management, high-volume saline irrigation and an intranasal steroid as first-line treatment, a culture-directed antibiotic only for an acute exacerbation with pus and no oral steroid for disease without polyps, CT of the sinuses only after appropriate medical therapy, the appropriateness criteria for endoscopic sinus surgery and a shared decision about it, and aviation medicine: sinus and ear barotrauma, not flying while symptomatic, a 48-hour ground trial of new medicines, which medicines the FAA accepts for pilots, and return to flying after surgery, on the AAO-HNS adult sinusitis guideline (1912 update), the ICAR rhinosinusitis consensus (1918), the RAND/UCLA appropriateness criteria for sinus surgery, and the FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners.
